title: John Marrero's chord style and Guesnon's single-string solos
summary: Marrero stuck to orchestration chords; Guesnon says he outdid his teacher by taking single-string solos, which modern work demands.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: But Lawrence isn't here to talk about him anymore. And you're one of the few people that really could describe. Did he play mostly the chord style? Just say four beats to a major. Did he put in extra beats?

Oh no, yeah, yeah, yeah, he was a wonderful chord man, but you see the question of it is he stuck close to the orchestration. In other words, he told me this when I went to take lessons for him. He said, George, no matter where you go, if you go play with a guy tonight, and this guy's got a piece of music that you don't have, copy the chords down so you go home and you'll memorize the chords that's on the orchestration. Because they're only true chords, and these are the kind of chords you must stay by. Only depend on your ear when there's no music around. He says, but when you can take a finer part, you can write those chords off and make sure you take those chords. And play them chords all the time, he says, and you'll find out that's where the real beauty of it lies. Because all arrangers know what they're doing. You see, they was getting away from strictly the ear music then. Stock numbers was coming in. And a guy had to sit down and do something with a part if he just couldn't master it to do something with it. You know what I mean? It was one of them thing.
Did he ever take many solos or one-string solos?

Well, no. You see, that's where I was better than he was. You see, that's what made me, as I say, I'm better than my teacher. As far as that goes. You see, my banjo playing today, that's what makes me stand out as a banjo player. It isn't that I make more chords than the other fella, or I read more better than him. I can solo more better than him. You see, I take all single-string solos. We'll say like Charlie Christian or somebody like that. And you get the beauty about taking all them broken-off pegs of yours and break them. And all such things as that. I mean, that's where when a man said take one, well, I mean, today you go. That possibly where some may differ and say it don't belong in the music, I'll agree to that, too. But today it's a demand. You take right now, I think one of the finest chord men in the business is Johnny St. Cyr. But he can't get a job because he cares solo. There isn't anything wrong with Johnny. I think Johnny's a fine musician and as great a chord man as they got anywhere in the country. But he cares solo. And today, if you don't take one, you ain't got no job. So you see, that was an issue that was forced upon you. Take one. Play the flute part. Play the heavy part. As long as you're able to take one. So that's why I had to change my style all around. And get away practically from too much rhythm and begin to be a solo banjo player. That's it.
